title: The conflict is disclosed
hook: Does a conflict warning automatically remove biased advice?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Separate disclosure from adviser behavior and recipient adjustment.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Separate disclosure from adviser behavior and recipient adjustment.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy adviser adds twenty units of bias to true value fifty. The recipient discounts five. What estimate remains? Toy inputs A=[50, 20, 5]; B=[50, 10, 0].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[65, 15, 50], [60, 10, 50]]. Labels: Recipient estimate, Residual bias, True value.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The disclosure case contains both a sender response and a recipient response. The net bias depends on their difference. Disclosure does not mechanically guarantee unbiased advice; these explicit toy responses are assumptions rather than measured behavior.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses True value=50, Adviser bias=10, Recipient discount=0. What is Recipient estimate? Answer: 60.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses True value=50, Adviser bias=10, Recipient discount=0. What is Recipient estimate?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 60. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.section: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceProvenance.text: Advisors who disclosed a conflict of interest gave more biased advice, and recipients didn't discount it enough (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore, 2005).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Separate disclosure from adviser behavior and recipient adjustment.
